newsitem.title: USA: Wis. governor, legislators spar over bonding veto.
newsitem.headline: Wis. governor, legislators spar over bonding veto.

text.p: The considerable veto powers of Wisconsin's governor will be the focus Tuesday of arguments before the state's high court by attorneys for Gov. Tommy Thompson and for a group of four legislators.

In January, the lawmakers, led by State Sen. Fred Risser, D-Madison, filed a petition with the court claiming Thompson had overstepped his constitutional veto powers when he decreased the amount of bonding authority in a transportation bill by $40 million.
The lawmakers' petition was aimed at action taken by Thompson in December, vetoing parts of the fiscal 1996-97 transportation budget bill that the legislature had passed in November.
The governor used his partial veto power to cross out $172.8 million of bonding authority, replacing it with $132.8 million of authorization, according to the petition.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court accepted the case on original jurisdiction in March, according to Michael Modl, a Madison, Wis., attorney representing Thompson and Secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Administration James Klauser.
Key to the legislators' case was a June 1995 ruling by the state high court that involved a challenge to a gubernatorial veto that removed and replaced an appropriation amount.
In their 4 to 3 ruling, justices limited such a veto move to appropriations only, allowing the governor to excise appropriation amounts in bills and replace them with lessor numbers.
Lynn Adelman, a Milwaukee attorney and a Democratic state senator from Waterford, who is representing the lawmakers, has said that bonding is not an appropriation, but an authorization.

In fact, the lawmakers' petition stated that Thompson, in his veto message, said he exercised the veto "not because the amounts vetoed were appropriation amounts, but because he objected to the authorized level of borrowing."
Modl said Thompson's position has been that the June 1995 state supreme court ruling also covers veto actions such as the one the governor took on the bonding in the transportation bill.

Additionally, Modl said that even if the bonding authorization was not considered an appropriation, the governor was able to take the veto action because the bonding authorization was contained in an appropriations bill.
Modl said the state supreme court could rule on the matter as early as December.
